notes.h: Housing requirements of families and single people
notes.b: A home that suits one household can be unworkable for another. Each group needs its own mix of space, location, access and services, and in an exam you should say who each requirement serves and why.
points: Families need enough bedrooms for every member, adequate storage, a well-equipped, ventilated and well-lit kitchen, and a living room for relaxing and watching television, so that everyone has space for their own needs.
A larger family also needs more than one bathroom, and a hot-press (an airing cupboard for the hot water tank and linen) helps with laundry.

Families with young children need a safe, enclosed back garden so the children can play outdoors without danger, and safe stairs. Teenagers need space to study, and families with a car or sports equipment may need a garage or shed.
Families also need to be close to schools, childcare, shops, parks and public transport, which cuts the time and cost of daily journeys for school-going children and working parents.

Single people usually need smaller, affordable accommodation, such as an apartment, bedsit, small townhouse or a room in a shared house, because they have one income. It should be close to work, college or public transport, with privacy, security and space for study.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the needs of named groups, such as families, single people, older people, people with disabilities and homeless people. Give six to eight distinct requirements, each tied to its group, for example a ramp lets a wheelchair user enter, a flashing doorbell alerts a person who cannot hear.

notes.h: Housing requirements of older people and people with disabilities
notes.b: For these groups the home itself must be adapted, because stairs, steps and standard fittings can make an ordinary house unsafe or unusable.
points: Older people need single-storey living living, or a ground-floor bedroom and bathroom, or a stairlift where there are stairs, because climbing stairs becomes difficult. They need a level or ramped entrance and non-slip floors with safe lighting to prevent falls.

Older people also need a home that is warm, well insulated and easy to heat, an alarm or emergency call system, and nearness to shops, health services, public transport and community and family support. Sheltered housing (accommodation designed for older people) is one option.

People with disabilities need adjustments that depend on the disability. For mobility: ramps for wheelchair or walking-aid users, wide doorways and hallways, lowered worktops, lowered switches and sockets at reachable heights, a raised toilet with grab rails, an accessible bathroom or shower, and a lift or stairlift.

For a hearing disability, flashing lights are linked to the doorbell and alarms, so the person is alerted without hearing a sound. For a sight disability, audible or tactile alarms and good lighting help, and communication or alarm systems are needed for emergencies.
notes.tip: Say which disability each adjustment serves, since the adjustments depend on the disability.

notes.b: Homeless people first need somewhere safe to stay tonight, and the aim is then a permanent home with support.
points: Homeless people need emergency shelter in hostels or emergency bed and breakfast accommodation, ideally regular rather than a nightly queue for a bed, with washing and laundry facilities, privacy and dignity, a safe place to store possessions and a communal space (kitchen or day room) to reduce isolation.
For homeless people the next step is rent-assisted private accommodation or local authority housing, and then a permanent home with support.
Serviced halting sites (sites with water and other services) exist for Travellers who live in mobile homes or caravans.
notes.tip: For homeless people, give four distinct points when asked, such as emergency shelter, washing facilities, privacy and a route to a permanent home.

notes.b: The State and voluntary bodies provide homes for people who cannot afford to buy or rent privately. Several routes exist, and each works differently.
points: Local authority housing is rented housing for households on a lower income who cannot afford a home. It is allocated by need through a social housing assessment and a waiting list, with priority given to households unable to house themselves.

Local authorities consider household size, income, current accommodation, age and disability. Families, people with disabilities and older people are often given priority, so single people can wait longer.

Voluntary housing is provided by approved housing bodies (non-profit voluntary organisations), often for specific groups such as older people, people with disabilities or homeless people. The tenant's landlord is the approved housing body.

Co-operative housing is built by a group of members who pool the costs of the site, builder and solicitor, share costs and manage the housing on non-profit principles. A local authority may provide a low-cost site for a co-operative whose members are on its waiting list.

The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) is a local authority support for private rented housing: the local authority pays the private landlord and the tenant pays a contribution. The Rental Accommodation Scheme (RAS) is where the local authority arranges long-term private rented homes for households with a long-term need.

Cost rental means homes let at a rent based on cost rather than profit, for households above social housing income limits. Do not confuse it with social housing (let at subsidised rent) or with affordable housing (sold below market price).

Shared equity and affordable purchase: under the First Home scheme the State and participating lenders take an equity share in a new home, which the buyer can buy out later. Local authorities also sell affordable homes below market price.

Adaptation grants help older people and people with disabilities to adapt a home so they can stay in it, and specific provision exists for homeless people, older people and Travellers. Demand for social housing exceeds supply, so applicants can wait for a number of years for a home.
notes.tip: If asked to name and give details of one type of social housing, choose local authority, approved housing body or co-operative housing and describe who provides it, who it is for and how it is allocated. Supports such as HAP, RAS, cost rental, allocation by need, waiting lists and adaptation grants also earn credit.

notes.b: Distribution is about where homes are and in what tenure (the way a home is held: owned, rented privately or rented from a social landlord). It is separate from whether those homes meet need.
points: By tenure, homes are owner-occupied (with a mortgage or owned outright), privately rented or socially rented from a local authority or approved housing body. Owner-occupation is the largest tenure in Ireland, followed by private renting and social housing.

By sector, private housing is built by developers and sold or let on the open market, while social housing is built and allocated by local authorities and approved housing bodies for people who cannot afford a home.
By location, urban areas have higher density, more apartments and greater demand, while rural areas have one-off houses and bungalows and, in some places, vacant homes.

Strong demand in cities and commuter areas pushes up prices and rents, while some rural areas have vacant housing but fewer jobs and services, so empty homes do not solve the shortage where people want to live.
notes.tip: Keep distribution (where homes are and in what tenure) separate from adequacy (whether they meet need) when you answer.

notes.b: A home can exist and still be a poor place to live. Quality is judged by structure and repair, insulation and heating, damp and ventilation, lighting, space for the household, safety and facilities.
points: A Building Energy Rating (BER) certificate rates a home's energy efficiency from A, the most efficient, to G, the least efficient, so buyers and tenants can compare running costs.
Older housing stock is often poorly insulated and costly to heat, which can cause fuel poverty (being unable to afford to heat the home adequately). New homes must meet the Building Regulations.
Damp, poor ventilation and inadequate lighting reduce the quality of accommodation and can affect health. Cold and overcrowding also harm health, and school and work performance.
Rented housing must meet legal minimum standards under the Housing (Standards for Rented Houses) Regulations 2019, which local authorities enforce.

notes.h: Comparative costs of buying and renting
notes.b: Buying and renting both cost money, but at different times and with different returns. Comparing them means looking at initial costs, ongoing costs and what you are left with.
points: Buying has initial costs: a deposit, legal fees, lender, valuation and survey fees, stamp duty on the purchase, and furnishing.

Buying has ongoing costs: mortgage repayments, mortgage protection and home insurance, property tax, maintenance and repairs, and service charges for apartments. It builds equity (the part of the home you own), may rise in value and gives security.
Renting has initial costs of a deposit (a month's rent is the usual) and rent in advance, and an agency fee where an agent is used. Ongoing costs are rent, contents insurance and utilities.
The tenant has no repair costs but builds no equity, so rent is sometimes called dead money. Renting needs less upfront capital and gives mobility, with lower upfront costs than buying.

In high-demand urban areas, rent can be as high as, or higher than, mortgage repayments on a similar home, so renting for years can cost more than buying, but buying requires a deposit that many people cannot save.
Rural homes are often cheaper to buy than urban ones, but residents may have to travel further to reach schools, shops and jobs.
notes.tip: Cost comparisons are rewarded for covering initial costs, ongoing costs and a balanced conclusion, so finish by weighing the two.

notes.h: Adequacy of housing provision (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Adequacy asks whether the housing on offer matches what households need. It goes beyond counting dwellings.
points: Adequacy means housing must be enough in number, affordable, secure, suitable, accessible, in good condition and near employment, transport, schools, healthcare and shops, for each type of household.

Strengths include a wide variety of house types and tenures, social housing through local authorities, approved housing bodies and co-operatives, cost rental, rent supports (HAP and RAS), supports for first-time buyers, adaptation grants, and better standards through the Building Regulations and the BER.

Weaknesses include high prices and rents in cities, waiting lists for social housing, homelessness, poor access for some people with disabilities and older people, poor stock in places, vacant property, and uneven distribution between urban and rural areas.
Emergency accommodation does not offer the stability of a permanent home, and long stays in it are a weakness.

Low-income families, lone parents, single people (lower priority for social housing), homeless people, Travellers, older people, people with disabilities, students and new arrivals (refugees and asylum seekers) may not get housing suited to their needs.
Local authority building, voluntary and co-operative schemes increase supply, and adaptation grants help particular groups to stay in their homes.
Renovating vacant property and planning mixed, serviced developments are further ways to improve adequacy, along with more social, affordable and cost rental homes and planning for need.
notes.tip: Name the sector or group first, then say how provision does or does not meet its need. Include a strength and a weakness of the owner-occupied, private rented and social sectors and the groups not well served, such as single people, homeless people, older people, Travellers and students. Treat adequacy in the wider sense of affordability, location and quality.

notes.b: A house is only as useful as what is around it. Amenities and services meet daily needs, and an estate without them isolates its residents.
points: Schools, childcare and playgrounds serve children and reduce long journeys for families.
Shops, post offices, banks, health services, pharmacies and community centres provide necessities and social contact, which builds a sense of community.
Public transport gives access to employment and services, so a development without transport isolates its residents.
Parks, sports grounds and play areas promote exercise, leisure and community interaction.
Street lighting improves safety, and regular refuse collection keeps the area hygienic.
Accessible healthcare, pharmacies and services for older people or people with disabilities support independence.
Setting: a group housing study of a local area such as a townland, village or housing estate, recording which amenities are present and which are missing.
notes.tip: Link each amenity to a need and to its effect on the community, for example lighting for safety and refuse collection for hygiene.

keyTerms.definition: Housing provided at subsidised rents or costs for households in need, through local authorities, approved housing bodies or co-operatives.
A household that owns the home it lives in and is paying off a mortgage on it or has paid it off.
Housing built and managed by a group of members who pool their resources to share the costs of site, builder and professional services.
A scheme, such as First Home, in which the State and lenders own a share of a new home alongside the buyer, who can buy out that share later.
A situation in which a household cannot afford to heat its home adequately, often because of poor insulation or outdated heating.
The extent to which housing supply meets the needs of different groups in terms of affordability, suitability, accessibility and location.
Temporary shelter, such as a hostel or emergency bed and breakfast, provided to people who have no home.
Facilities such as schools, shops, transport, parks and healthcare that make a housing development a place to live.
A non-profit body approved to provide social housing, often for particular groups such as older people or people with disabilities.

factCards.term: Three ways a family's housing needs differ from a single person's
factCards.definition: More bedrooms and storage; a safe enclosed garden for young children; space for a car or sports equipment.

factCards.term: Four home adjustments for people with disabilities
factCards.definition: Ramps for wheelchair or walking-aid users; lowered switches and sockets; flashing visual alarms; an accessible bathroom.
Local authority housing; voluntary housing provided by approved housing bodies; co-operative housing built by a group of members.

factCards.term: Four facilities a new housing development should provide
factCards.definition: Schools and childcare; shops and services; public transport; play areas and parks.

factCards.term: Two reasons older housing can be costly to heat
factCards.definition: Poor insulation and draughts; outdated or inefficient heating systems.

factCards.term: Stage of homelessness support that follows emergency shelter
factCards.definition: Rent-assisted private accommodation, leading on to a permanent home.

questions.prompt: Name and describe two features a home should have to meet the needs of an older person living alone.
questions.model: Single-storey living or a stairlift, so that the person can reach all rooms safely without climbing stairs; level or ramped entrances and step-free access; a home that is warm and easy to heat, with good insulation; a location close to shops, health services and public transport. Any two features, each named and described, earn the marks.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the adequacy of housing provision in Ireland today for families, single people and homeless people.
questions.model: Adequacy means affordable, secure, suitable, accessible and well located housing. Families: adequate space, bedrooms and storage, and safe outdoor space; provision is limited in cities where large family homes are scarce and expensive. Single people: smaller, affordable accommodation such as apartments and private rented homes is available in urban areas, but rents are high and shared accommodation can be poor quality. Homeless people: emergency accommodation such as hostels and emergency bed and breakfast provides shelter but not the stability of a home; move-on supports such as rent-assisted private accommodation help some people, but long social housing waiting lists and the limited supply of permanent homes leave many in emergency accommodation. Overall distribution: strong demand in cities and commuter areas and vacancy in some rural areas; social provision by local authorities, approved housing bodies and co-operatives helps, but supply does not meet demand. Quality: older stock is costly to heat and may be damp, so some homes are not adequate. A balanced evaluation should reach a conclusion on which groups are best and worst served.
